title:
CLO International Academic Month Issue 3 (Part 2)  
The Application of CLO3D at Sigmaringen University of Applied Sciences
description: In this issue's academic monthly video, Professor Christian Kaiser from Sigmaringen University of Applied Sciences shares the practical application of CLO3D in everyday fashion teaching. As an engineering professor, his interdisciplinary teaching experience demonstrates the potential for CLO3D software to be applied in other fields. After the course, students took on challenges using the software and designed many cool works! Click the video to watch!
transcript:
Okay, Professor Kaeser, we can start now whenever you are ready.  
Okay, thank you.  
So I'm going to share my screen.  
Perfect.  
You can see it.  
Yeah, I can see it.  
Okay, awesome.  
So yeah.  
Thank you very much.  
I would like to welcome all of you also from my side.  
Um, I guess I have already been introduced.  
My name is Christian Kaiser.  
I am a professor at the University of Albstadt-Sigmaringen in the textile department.  
We educate textile and garment engineers.  
My scientific background is that I am an engineering cybernetician, which actually means that I am a control engineer or systems engineer,  
and I came into contact with textile topics during my studies at the University of Stuttgart.  
What I would like to give you is a short overview and some insights into how our university introduced CLO 3D into our curriculum.  
Because before I joined Albstadt-Sigmaringen University in 2018, 3D was not a focus point in our teaching classes.  
My personal background: I have been a 3D user since 2010, so I would say one of the first users in Europe.  
And actually, as I am not from the garment and textile industry, it was not hard to convince myself,  
because if you look at mechanical engineering, aerospace, and all other mechanical engineering disciplines,  
3D development and 3D simulation is state of the art.  
So to me, it’s pretty obvious that 3D development and 3D visualization of garments is also something  
that should be implemented in the future.  
And I hope that we can do that in the textile industry as soon as possible.  

Starting with what we did to implement 3D classes based on CLO in our bachelor’s degree,  
the starting point was the winter semester 2019/2020.  
There, we started introducing 3D models.  
We started using CLO 3D within our bachelor courses.  
Actually, at this time, it started with one course.  
And pretty soon, a colleague of mine, who is a designer, and I,  
we attended the CLO academic workshop in Munich, Germany.  
This was our start, where we refined our  
already pre-existing understanding of 3D simulation with this type of software.  
Both of us were skilled in terms of other software,  
because we use multiple 3D software at our university.  
But this workshop was really a kind of game changer,  
because after that, we could really speed up our tutorial database,  
our online courses, as well as enhance the quality of our in-person teaching.  
Pretty soon after this, we also had our first student 3D project in 2020,  
and our second one in the very next semester.  
After this, we started optimizing our tutorial database.  
Perhaps something I should tell you, because I am a control engineer,  
I personally live in a feedback loop,  
which means every kind of teaching, every type of action I am responsible for,  
starts with some kind of steering impulse,  
which means starting with curriculum and stuff like this.  
And we optimize each of our lectures on a regular basis,  
based on the feedback of the students,  
based on developments in the market,  
be it software-wise or application-wise.  
This means that by mid-2021,  
we had our first big run-through,  
which we used to optimize our tutorial database,  
and also went for a second academic workshop at CLO in Munich.  
In fact, for us, the second workshop wasn’t that necessary anymore,  
because we were already quite skilled in what we were doing,  
but twofold,  
this was super helpful.  
The first part is networking.  
I guess all of you have experienced that 3D,  
even though it’s not that new anymore,  
is still an area of teaching where we lack routine.  
The other part is that there are very active, highly skilled players.  
And if you want to push forward,  
it’s very helpful to build your own network,  
whether in industry or in the academic world.  
This is the reason why we attended the CLO academic workshop again in 2021.  
Once again, because this helped us to go to the next level.  

What were the challenges we faced?  
The main challenge is embedding 3D into current curricula.  
Because I guess all of you have experienced this issue.  
You already have existing lessons.  
And you have to focus on the areas that are important to you,  
be it sewing,  
textiles,  
CAD,  
or 3D,  
which is something new entering the curriculum,  
meaning you really have to focus.  
For us, the general focus points were,  
first of all, mechanics,  
digital sewing,  
and then two application areas:  
virtual fit and the 3D design part.  

What you see on the right side is work from my students in 2021,  
where they, based on the materials I was teaching them,  
had to experience their own small projects,  
like developing a 2D pattern,  
transferring the data—  
in this case, we used Electra’s 2D system to CLO—  
to arrange patterns,  
do the first fittings,  
then debug,  
optimize the draping of the garment,  
optimize the pattern sizes to the fit,  
and also identify—  
this is something you can see on the shirt of Gabriela Schön, summer semester 2020, on the backside—  
which areas have inconsistencies,  
or the other part,  
we link this also to our sewing classes,  
equivalent to what you face in real life.  

I already talked about embedding 3D.  
And I really choose this word on purpose,  
which means embedding is something different from an add-on.  
What I face in European teaching is that many universities  
understand 3D skills as add-ons to traditional textile and garment skills.  
In my opinion,  
this point of view is quite mistaken.  
It’s not an add-on;  
it’s a basic skill.  
Just as students are able to sew,  
as they are able to develop patterns by hand,  
and build up other competencies,  
3D is a standard skill.  

This means that our students do not have a choice  
when it comes to 3D classes for quite a long time.  
The skills we really want to transfer to our students mean that in the bachelor’s degree,  
we have digital construction lessons,  
which are split between pattern,  
pattern meaning construction by hand,  
CAD,  
meaning computer-aided design construction,  
and the 3D simulation of exactly these CAD patterns.  

This allows the students to have a close feedback loop.  
What I develop by hand,  
I see how to do on the computer,  
and I see the result of the drape in 3D on a defined human model.  
We do this on a standard level in Digital Construction 2,  
and go into more advanced 2D and 3D skills in Digital Construction 3.  
In Digital Construction 4,  
we shift focus.  
There, we go into high-end simulation and rendering,  
because having digital twins of your garments on the technical part is one thing,  
enabling visual communication and high-end visual communication is another very important part.  

Having this so far enables  
students to use 3D as a standard skill in projects.  
These projects might be project lectures,  
but also projects they have in different lectures.  
For example,  
we have lectures focusing on more uncommon sewing and tufting solutions,  
like welding,  
like gluing, and such,  
where the students, for example, work on rain jackets.  

Since we started implementing this type of curriculum,  
the students use 3D for 3D prototyping  
of the garments they develop in this lecture on their own.  
This means 3D is a real standard skill.  
And the professor who has this lecture  
is actually not a 3D expert.  
He also did not push the students to do so,  
but it was the students’ own choice to do that.  

And this is something that makes me really proud,  
because regularly you try to push industry exactly in this way,  
like an industrial garment manufacturer,  
please do digital prototyping first before you go to the real prototype.  
And that’s something my students really do on their own initiative.  
For sure,  
I have to admit that for the more advanced lectures,  
we really pushed the students  
and raised awareness about this.  
But now, it’s the students adopting and using these skills themselves.  

I would say 3D is a standard skill for our students,  
a standard skill at the latest by the third semester,  
which they can use in further lectures such as design lectures,  
3D print design,  
3D knit design,  
alternative sewing technologies, and others.  

I already mentioned another success factor: the CLO academic workshop.  
For me personally,  
it was less about teaching the mechanics of the 3D software,  
but more about the excellent tutorial database.  
I mean, the CAD database that CLO provides in these workshops,  
because this really helped me build tutorials and curricula for my students  
in a very lean and handy way,  
and expand these teaching materials according to my purpose.  
So I really recommend you take advantage of offers like this.  
These are super, super helpful.  

Another success factor in our case is the team.  
I guess you already heard I’m more the techie.  
So design and aesthetics are by far not my core competencies.  
I don’t care if a shirt is pink or yellow when it comes to the technical part,  
because for me,  
it’s just the question:  
Did you do your job on a technical basis correctly or not?  

My colleague, Maria Baum,  
she’s the creative part.  
She is a design professor.  
She really helps the students to use the means and tools I teach them in a super creative way to realize very difficult or innovative designs.  
Which means we complement each other as enablers and can accompany the students at the right level,  
to have the best learning experience depending on the type of application you are looking at.  

The other part is that I built an online teaching platform for all the software we use in our textile classes at our university  
with video tutorials.  
I would say pure conviction: Marina and I are super convinced that it’s not a question of whether you do 3D,  
it’s just a question of how well you do it,  
because it is, in my opinion, one of the most important tools for industry for the next five to ten years.  

The other part, and this was even more important during Corona,  
was to enable the students in the best way possible to choose their own learning experience.  
This is something we optimize regularly,  
like each semester we enhance and improve our tutorial database,  
our scripts, and our teaching materials for in-person lessons and teaching.  

Here you see a very simple example for a 3D design class.  
I guess all of you face, more or less, the trust issue in industry:  
Does 3D have any positive impact on my work or not?  
In this case, you just see a regular T-shirt,  
what we call a “white shell,”  
which we draped with different textures like mesh, knit, jersey, shiny textures,  
and you see that the appearance of the T-shirts completely depends on the type of material you use.  

This is something I really focus on making the students understand,  
because if you are, for example, a T-shirt or trousers manufacturer,  
if you are capable of building up white shell libraries,  
this really speeds up your processes.  

Okay, this is like light-speed compared to what is done so far,  
because so far, industry either works on swatches or makes prototypes,  
including the latency you need until these prototypes are manufactured.  
And by this, it’s just like a drag-and-drop operation having these designs.  

For a skilled student of mine, and I guess also for skilled students of yours,  
it’s like minutes once you have your simulation, and even building the simulation is a matter of minutes, not hours.  

What I also teach the students is the ingredients of a good simulation.  
We are aware of the fabric,  
we are aware of the pattern,  
we are aware of the human model, like the 3D human model,  
and when it comes to fabric,  
we teach the students the different types of maps and their uses,  
and how to improve them:  
sharp maps that are not blurry, that are brilliant for later high-end rendering, or  
option two, you are just sketching, use your smartphone or any other camera, have a short video snippet,  
and assess the worth of the design or not.  

Here you also see work of my students.  
Actually, all the things you see here are student work from 2021.  
My students are now much better than they were at that time,  
but we also use multiple tools surrounding the traditional 2D CAD tools in 3D.  

For example, Fusion 360 here:  
we made buckles and similar items.  
We also work with Blender  
to bring hardware components together,  
for example, some kind of carabiner.  
And we bring all of that together in CLO, for example, in the bachelor classes,  
to make the students understand how to make hardware and trims if you don’t have them,  
how to import different formats like OBJ, FBX, GLTF from other frameworks into the 3D simulation framework.  

Because this is also based on my systems engineering background:  
you have to think in frameworks.  
The best software not being framework-capable, or you don’t use it in a framework, is just a digitalization of one step,  
but it’s about how to digitize the entire steps you face and need.  

Here you see work in progress, how the students improve from their sketch to the final simulation.  
This is something we closely accompany with our students and teach them how to do this,  
but most of the time it’s based on their own projects after standard teaching.  

Here you see what we used as a basis:  
for example, the carabiner was from Avatar,  
the pattern pieces were garments,  
and for example here, the button was used as a trim.  

Here you see other student project results:  
This is a backpack simulated in CLO,  
which we later rendered in KeyShot, because  
I also want my students to understand you can do high-end visualization within 3D tools,  
but I think also, much more expensive with 3D,  
there are options to further enhance your work outside the traditional 3D garment tools.  

The question is, depending on your application, which type of visualization quality you need.  
Being honest, CLO is always super fast, and your visualizations are really good.  
If you want to go for the last percent, others might also be of use.  

Here you also see a different type of bags.  
Focusing on garments does not mean leaving out other textile products.  
For example, this semester we started a lecture where students develop a backpack in 3D and also manufacture this backpack in 3D,  
without sewing, just with gluing and welding,  
to really push forward the idea of digital prototyping and advanced manufacturing techniques.  

Here you see another example of one of my students’ work, also from 2020.  
This is something I am very proud of,  
because you see here the students had the task to develop digital and technical marketing purposes within their project.  

And you see here on the right side of the puffer jacket,  
you clearly see the funnels of the down filling,  
which is very hard to visualize when doing real manufacturing or prototyping,  
but is super easy when using 3D simulation of garments.  

This was one of the best student works at that time.  
I am really happy about it,  
the creativity, the detail level of the simulation, as well as the ideas on how to present the products.  

We also focus on knits because weft and warp knitting is one of the focus teaching areas at our university as well.  
I think I have to tell you that at Albstadt we are in a knitting cluster in southern Germany,  
which means we have machine manufacturers for weft and warp knitting right next door.  

I guess you all know that visualization of knitted garments is like the Champions League of 3D visualization.  
You see there are inconsistencies when it comes to the gradient from the mesh of the weft knitting on this part to the ribs on that part.  
I guess you know this issue; most customers don’t.  

What you also see is that you can really go to high-end visualization.  
And if you don’t know it’s a simulation,  
I think it comes pretty close to what you can also show to the end customer, especially when you go, for example, to web visualization like 720p.  

These are other examples of my students’ work.  
Here’s some rain jackets.  
There’s some training and competition outfits.  
Most of the time, especially if the students are skilled in later semesters,  
they just get a task to simulate garments that have a certain level of difficulty,  
and the type of garment is their choice.  

In this case, it was sportswear, the main topic.  
It’s the students’ choice.  
And if you look at the taping, for example,  
I think it’s brilliant what this student did in this case.  

You can also do super fancy 3D presentations.  
You don’t always have to think in the traditional style,  
but can really enhance your creativity.  
This is something I really encourage myself.  

Thank you.  
And now I ask some very classic questions.  
Let’s try to put a few head-on here to the camera  
so that the shameless person  
can see these match my students’ efforts to push their limits, push their ideas, and also  
push the software to get a better understanding of what is possible so far.  

This is something my students did in 2021.  
So this is something the industry is trying to achieve right now, and I can tell you it’s possible.  
If my students can do this, industry hardware—  
I don’t know.  
I don’t know.  
Yeah, actually, this was one of the clips my students did in the industry project 2020 to 2021.  
I guess you already see this was two years ago. And this is what this type of students was already capable of.  

I take these roughly old examples to  
show how capable digital technology and 3D technology already was two to three years ago.  
Right now, we can achieve even more because computing power is better,  
the algorithms are better,  
which means the type of garments, the creativity, and the touch and feel you can realize is much better  
even now than what these students experienced in 2021.  

But if you look closely, I would say this is already brilliant.  
And I guess everyone can understand the value these technologies have in teaching.  
And I also think you can easily understand how proud my students were of their work once finished.  
And I think you can easily learn something new from this project,  
which means others can appreciate it too.  

Because I was so impressed with projects like this.  
These types of projects are industrial projects,  
which means in the sixth semester, pretty at the end of their studies,  
the students have 15 weeks’ target to work on an issue  
provided by industrial partners.  
They do this about 20 hours per week.  

And these are part of the results my students achieved in this context.  
Partner in this type of project. The task was to develop digital collections with full creativity  
and to do as much visualization as possible.  

One chart outlook is that in the digital world today is just like the tomorrow of yesterday, which means  
we really focus on improving our workflows.  
This means we consistently work on workflows.  
The one you see here is that we use Blender, Autodesk, Visu  
for asset generation.  
We do all this in the workflow of 2D pattern development  
as well as in Silhouette and do the 3D simulation there.  
And then you can just decide where to publish: for example, Unity,  
where you can build AR apps or 3D viewer apps.  
You can go for KeyShot for rendering.  
You can go for Blender as an intermediate renderer or tool,  
or you can render and publish directly from Silhouette.  

Right now, you have many innovative solutions in CLO,  
also since the last days when it comes to AR.  

This is one of our workflows.  
We work on many different workflows.  
We work on many different models.  
We work on multiple ones.  
And I really focus on making my students understand the value of these as well.  

Yeah, actually, from my part, that’s it.  
I really, really want to thank you for your attention.  
And I hope I could give some insights into our work,  
that I could inspire your work a little bit.  

And if you have any questions also in the next days or weeks, please feel free to ask them in the Q&A box.  
And if you have any questions also in the next days or weeks, please feel free to ask them in the Q&A box.  
And if you have any questions also in the next days or weeks,  
I guess Elaine will provide my contact data.  
Feel always free to get in touch and ask me.

CLO International Academic Month Issue 3 (Part 2)  
The Application of CLO3D at Sigmaringen University of Applied Sciences
chunks.content: ## Introduction to CLO 3D Implementation at Sigmaringen University This section introduces Professor Christian Kaiser from the University of Albstadt-Sigmaringen’s textile department, his background, and the initial steps taken to integrate CLO 3D software into the university’s curriculum. Key terms include CLO 3D, 3D simulation, textile education, and digital garment prototyping. Professor Christian Kaiser, an engineering cybernetician with a background in control and systems engineering, joined the University of Albstadt-Sigmaringen in 2018. Prior to his arrival, 3D garment simulation was not a focus in the textile and garment engineering curriculum. Having been an early adopter of 3D technology since 2010, Kaiser recognized the importance of integrating 3D development and visualization into textile education, paralleling advancements in mechanical engineering and aerospace industries. The university began incorporating CLO 3D into bachelor’s courses starting in the winter semester of 2019/2020, initially with a single course. Professor Kaiser and a design colleague attended the CLO academic workshop in Munich, which significantly enhanced their expertise and allowed them to develop a comprehensive tutorial database and improve in-person teaching quality. By 2020, students engaged in their first 3D projects, with ongoing curriculum optimization driven by student feedback and market developments. ## Curriculum Integration and Teaching Strategy for 3D Simulation This section details the challenges and strategies for embedding CLO 3D into existing textile and garment curricula. It covers course structure, feedback loops, and the importance of viewing 3D skills as foundational rather than supplementary. Embedding 3D simulation into the existing curriculum posed challenges, as traditional courses already covered sewing, textiles, and CAD. The university focused on mechanics, digital sewing, virtual fit, and 3D design applications. Students work on projects that involve developing 2D patterns using Electra’s CAD system, transferring these to CLO 3D, performing fittings, debugging, and optimizing garment drape and fit. They also learn to identify inconsistencies and relate 3D simulation results to physical sewing challenges. Professor Kaiser emphasizes that 3D skills should be considered a core competency in textile education, not an add-on. Students are required to take digital construction lessons that integrate hand pattern making, CAD pattern construction, and 3D simulation. This approach creates a feedback loop where students see the correlation between hand development, CAD design, and 3D draping on human models. The curriculum progresses through levels: Digital Construction 2 covers standard 3D simulation, Digital Construction 3 advances 2D and 3D skills, and Digital Construction 4 focuses on high-end simulation and rendering for digital twins and visual communication. 3D simulation is integrated as a standard skill by the third semester and is utilized in various lectures including design, 3D print design, 3D knit design, and alternative sewing technologies. Notably, students independently apply 3D prototyping in non-3D expert-led courses, demonstrating the skill’s permeation into their learning. ## Importance of CLO Academic Workshops and Team Collaboration This section highlights the significance of attending CLO academic workshops and the complementary roles within the teaching team. It also covers the development of supporting online teaching materials.

CLO International Academic Month Issue 3 (Part 2)  
The Application of CLO3D at Sigmaringen University of Applied Sciences
chunks.content: 3D simulation is integrated as a standard skill by the third semester and is utilized in various lectures including design, 3D print design, 3D knit design, and alternative sewing technologies. Notably, students independently apply 3D prototyping in non-3D expert-led courses, demonstrating the skill’s permeation into their learning. ## Importance of CLO Academic Workshops and Team Collaboration This section highlights the significance of attending CLO academic workshops and the complementary roles within the teaching team. It also covers the development of supporting online teaching materials. Attending the CLO academic workshops was crucial not only for mastering software mechanics but also for accessing CLO’s extensive tutorial and CAD databases, which facilitated efficient curriculum and tutorial development. Networking at these workshops helped connect with active experts in both academic and industry settings, supporting continuous advancement in teaching quality. The teaching team combines technical and creative expertise: Professor Kaiser focuses on technical and systems aspects, while his colleague Maria Baum, a design professor, guides students on creative and aesthetic applications. This complementary partnership enhances the learning experience across different applications. An online teaching platform with video tutorials was created to support student learning across the software tools used in textile classes. This platform allows students to choose their own learning pace and style, which became especially important during remote learning periods such as the COVID-19 pandemic. The teaching materials and tutorials are regularly updated and refined each semester. ## Practical Applications and Student Projects Using CLO 3D This section describes specific student projects, practical applications of CLO 3D, and how material properties and digital prototyping accelerate design workflows. It also covers the integration of additional 3D tools and formats. Students engage in projects that involve the creation of 3D garment prototypes, such as T-shirts, rain jackets, backpacks, puffer jackets, and sportswear. A key teaching point is understanding how different fabric textures and materials (e.g., mesh, knit, jersey, shiny textures) affect the appearance and behavior of garments in simulation. Creating "white shell" libraries of base garments accelerates design iteration by enabling rapid drag-and-drop texture application and fitting. The use of 3D simulation drastically reduces the time and resources compared to traditional prototyping, which relies on physical swatches and sample production. Students are taught the components of effective simulation: accurate fabric properties, precise pattern data, and reliable 3D human models. They learn about various texture maps and their impact on rendering quality, from high-end sharp maps suitable for photorealistic visualization to quick sketches captured by smartphones for design assessment. Additional 3D tools such as Fusion 360 and Blender are incorporated for designing hardware components like buckles and carabiners. Students learn how to import various 3D file formats (OBJ, FBX, GLTF) into CLO to assemble complex garment models with trims and accessories. Student projects evolve from initial sketches to fully simulated garments, with examples including detailed backpacks and digitally rendered collections. High-end rendering is performed using tools like KeyShot, augmenting CLO’s visualization capabilities when ultra-realistic images are required.

chunks.title:
CLO International Academic Month Issue 3 (Part 2)  
The Application of CLO3D at Sigmaringen University of Applied Sciences
chunks.content: Additional 3D tools such as Fusion 360 and Blender are incorporated for designing hardware components like buckles and carabiners. Students learn how to import various 3D file formats (OBJ, FBX, GLTF) into CLO to assemble complex garment models with trims and accessories. Student projects evolve from initial sketches to fully simulated garments, with examples including detailed backpacks and digitally rendered collections. High-end rendering is performed using tools like KeyShot, augmenting CLO’s visualization capabilities when ultra-realistic images are required. ## Advanced Manufacturing Techniques and Visualization of Textile Products This section covers the application of 3D simulation beyond traditional garments, including digital prototyping of backpacks using advanced manufacturing techniques like gluing and welding. It also discusses visualization challenges specific to knitted textiles and training students in industry-relevant workflows. The curriculum has expanded to include innovative product types such as backpacks manufactured without sewing, using gluing and welding techniques. This pushes digital prototyping and manufacturing into advanced realms. Knitwear visualization presents particular challenges due to complex mesh gradients and stitch types (weft and warp knitting). The university leverages its proximity to knitting machine manufacturers to emphasize this area. The high-quality 3D renderings produced approximate real textile appearance closely, suitable even for customer-facing visualizations at resolutions like 720p. Students also simulate complex sportswear and competition outfits, demonstrating advanced taping and garment detailing. Encouragement is given to explore creative and non-traditional 3D presentation styles to enhance innovation. ## Industrial Collaboration and Workflow Optimization This section describes industrial projects completed by students, the timeframes involved, and the digital workflows employed to integrate various tools and platforms for 3D garment development and visualization. In the sixth semester, students participate in 15-week industry projects, dedicating approximately 20 hours per week to address real-world challenges provided by industrial partners. These projects focus on creating digital collections with full creative freedom and extensive visualization. The university emphasizes continuous workflow optimization, combining 2D pattern development with 3D simulation and asset generation using tools like Blender, Autodesk, and Visu. The digital assets are then published across platforms such as Unity (for augmented reality and 3D viewers), KeyShot (for rendering), Blender (as an intermediate rendering tool), or directly from Silhouette. Recent CLO updates, including AR capabilities, have expanded the possibilities for visualization and presentation. ## Summary and Outlook This final section reflects on the progress made at the University of Albstadt-Sigmaringen with CLO 3D integration, the growing capabilities of students, and the anticipated importance of 3D technology in the textile industry. Projects completed as far back as 2020-2021 demonstrate that students are capable of producing high-quality digital garments and visualizations, indicating that 3D technology is mature enough for broader industry adoption. Advances in computing power and algorithms continue to enhance the realism and creativity achievable in digital garment simulation. Professor Kaiser underscores that 3D skills are essential for textile engineers and that the university’s approach equips students to meet future industry needs.

CLO International Academic Month Issue 3 (Part 2)  
The Application of CLO3D at Sigmaringen University of Applied Sciences
chunks.content: ## Summary and Outlook This final section reflects on the progress made at the University of Albstadt-Sigmaringen with CLO 3D integration, the growing capabilities of students, and the anticipated importance of 3D technology in the textile industry. Projects completed as far back as 2020-2021 demonstrate that students are capable of producing high-quality digital garments and visualizations, indicating that 3D technology is mature enough for broader industry adoption. Advances in computing power and algorithms continue to enhance the realism and creativity achievable in digital garment simulation. Professor Kaiser underscores that 3D skills are essential for textile engineers and that the university’s approach equips students to meet future industry needs. markdown_content: ## Introduction to CLO 3D Implementation at Sigmaringen University This section introduces Professor Christian Kaiser from the University of Albstadt-Sigmaringen’s textile department, his background, and the initial steps taken to integrate CLO 3D software into the university’s curriculum. Key terms include CLO 3D, 3D simulation, textile education, and digital garment prototyping. Professor Christian Kaiser, an engineering cybernetician with a background in control and systems engineering, joined the University of Albstadt-Sigmaringen in 2018. Prior to his arrival, 3D garment simulation was not a focus in the textile and garment engineering curriculum. Having been an early adopter of 3D technology since 2010, Kaiser recognized the importance of integrating 3D development and visualization into textile education, paralleling advancements in mechanical engineering and aerospace industries. The university began incorporating CLO 3D into bachelor’s courses starting in the winter semester of 2019/2020, initially with a single course. Professor Kaiser and a design colleague attended the CLO academic workshop in Munich, which significantly enhanced their expertise and allowed them to develop a comprehensive tutorial database and improve in-person teaching quality. By 2020, students engaged in their first 3D projects, with ongoing curriculum optimization driven by student feedback and market developments. ## Curriculum Integration and Teaching Strategy for 3D Simulation This section details the challenges and strategies for embedding CLO 3D into existing textile and garment curricula. It covers course structure, feedback loops, and the importance of viewing 3D skills as foundational rather than supplementary. Embedding 3D simulation into the existing curriculum posed challenges, as traditional courses already covered sewing, textiles, and CAD. The university focused on mechanics, digital sewing, virtual fit, and 3D design applications. Students work on projects that involve developing 2D patterns using Electra’s CAD system, transferring these to CLO 3D, performing fittings, debugging, and optimizing garment drape and fit. They also learn to identify inconsistencies and relate 3D simulation results to physical sewing challenges. Professor Kaiser emphasizes that 3D skills should be considered a core competency in textile education, not an add-on. Students are required to take digital construction lessons that integrate hand pattern making, CAD pattern construction, and 3D simulation. This approach creates a feedback loop where students see the correlation between hand development, CAD design, and 3D draping on human models. The curriculum progresses through levels: Digital Construction 2 covers standard 3D simulation, Digital Construction 3 advances 2D and 3D skills, and Digital Construction 4 focuses on high-end simulation and rendering for digital twins and visual communication. 3D simulation is integrated as a standard skill by the third semester and is utilized in various lectures including design, 3D print design, 3D knit design, and alternative sewing technologies. Notably, students independently apply 3D prototyping in non-3D expert-led courses, demonstrating the skill’s permeation into their learning. ## Importance of CLO Academic Workshops and Team Collaboration This section highlights the significance of attending CLO academic workshops and the complementary roles within the teaching team. It also covers the development of supporting online teaching materials. Attending the CLO academic workshops was crucial not only for mastering software mechanics but also for accessing CLO’s extensive tutorial and CAD databases, which facilitated efficient curriculum and tutorial development. Networking at these workshops helped connect with active experts in both academic and industry settings, supporting continuous advancement in teaching quality. The teaching team combines technical and creative expertise: Professor Kaiser focuses on technical and systems aspects, while his colleague Maria Baum, a design professor, guides students on creative and aesthetic applications. This complementary partnership enhances the learning experience across different applications. An online teaching platform with video tutorials was created to support student learning across the software tools used in textile classes. This platform allows students to choose their own learning pace and style, which became especially important during remote learning periods such as the COVID-19 pandemic. The teaching materials and tutorials are regularly updated and refined each semester. ## Practical Applications and Student Projects Using CLO 3D This section describes specific student projects, practical applications of CLO 3D, and how material properties and digital prototyping accelerate design workflows. It also covers the integration of additional 3D tools and formats. Students engage in projects that involve the creation of 3D garment prototypes, such as T-shirts, rain jackets, backpacks, puffer jackets, and sportswear. A key teaching point is understanding how different fabric textures and materials (e.g., mesh, knit, jersey, shiny textures) affect the appearance and behavior of garments in simulation. Creating "white shell" libraries of base garments accelerates design iteration by enabling rapid drag-and-drop texture application and fitting. The use of 3D simulation drastically reduces the time and resources compared to traditional prototyping, which relies on physical swatches and sample production. Students are taught the components of effective simulation: accurate fabric properties, precise pattern data, and reliable 3D human models. They learn about various texture maps and their impact on rendering quality, from high-end sharp maps suitable for photorealistic visualization to quick sketches captured by smartphones for design assessment. Additional 3D tools such as Fusion 360 and Blender are incorporated for designing hardware components like buckles and carabiners. Students learn how to import various 3D file formats (OBJ, FBX, GLTF) into CLO to assemble complex garment models with trims and accessories. Student projects evolve from initial sketches to fully simulated garments, with examples including detailed backpacks and digitally rendered collections. High-end rendering is performed using tools like KeyShot, augmenting CLO’s visualization capabilities when ultra-realistic images are required. ## Advanced Manufacturing Techniques and Visualization of Textile Products This section covers the application of 3D simulation beyond traditional garments, including digital prototyping of backpacks using advanced manufacturing techniques like gluing and welding. It also discusses visualization challenges specific to knitted textiles and training students in industry-relevant workflows. The curriculum has expanded to include innovative product types such as backpacks manufactured without sewing, using gluing and welding techniques. This pushes digital prototyping and manufacturing into advanced realms. Knitwear visualization presents particular challenges due to complex mesh gradients and stitch types (weft and warp knitting). The university leverages its proximity to knitting machine manufacturers to emphasize this area. The high-quality 3D renderings produced approximate real textile appearance closely, suitable even for customer-facing visualizations at resolutions like 720p. Students also simulate complex sportswear and competition outfits, demonstrating advanced taping and garment detailing. Encouragement is given to explore creative and non-traditional 3D presentation styles to enhance innovation. ## Industrial Collaboration and Workflow Optimization This section describes industrial projects completed by students, the timeframes involved, and the digital workflows employed to integrate various tools and platforms for 3D garment development and visualization. In the sixth semester, students participate in 15-week industry projects, dedicating approximately 20 hours per week to address real-world challenges provided by industrial partners. These projects focus on creating digital collections with full creative freedom and extensive visualization. The university emphasizes continuous workflow optimization, combining 2D pattern development with 3D simulation and asset generation using tools like Blender, Autodesk, and Visu. The digital assets are then published across platforms such as Unity (for augmented reality and 3D viewers), KeyShot (for rendering), Blender (as an intermediate rendering tool), or directly from Silhouette. Recent CLO updates, including AR capabilities, have expanded the possibilities for visualization and presentation. ## Summary and Outlook This final section reflects on the progress made at the University of Albstadt-Sigmaringen with CLO 3D integration, the growing capabilities of students, and the anticipated importance of 3D technology in the textile industry. Projects completed as far back as 2020-2021 demonstrate that students are capable of producing high-quality digital garments and visualizations, indicating that 3D technology is mature enough for broader industry adoption. Advances in computing power and algorithms continue to enhance the realism and creativity achievable in digital garment simulation. Professor Kaiser underscores that 3D skills are essential for textile engineers and that the university’s approach equips students to meet future industry needs. The collaboration between technical and creative faculty, combined with robust teaching resources and industrial partnerships, positions graduates well for the evolving digital landscape. Contact information for further questions is made available to encourage continued dialogue and knowledge sharing.
